Knoxville by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 193,721 people in Knoxville, which makes it the 3rd largest of the 28 Tennessee places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $214,000, 23% below the median of those 28 places. 47% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 53% are rented, against a median of 61% owner-occupancy across the Tennessee places. The median home was built in 1974, about 49 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Knoxville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who bills property tax on a Knoxville house?

Two governments send a bill, and the Knox County Property Assessor sets the value behind both. A house inside the city limits owes Knox County tax and City of Knoxville tax, each collected by a different office. Keep the two bills separate, because the city says plainly that payments sent to the wrong office cause errors.

  • City bill: the City of Knoxville Revenue Office, phone 865-215-2084, Suite 453 of the City County Building at 400 Main Street, open weekdays, 8:00 to 4:30. Mail goes to P.O. Box 15001, Knoxville, TN 37901-5001.
  • County bill: the Knox County Trustee, phone 865-215-2305, Suite 427 of the same building, with matching weekday hours. Mail goes to P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901, and the Trustee runs six locations.
  • Value questions: the Knox County Property Assessor, 865-215-2360.
  • Deed questions: the Register of Deeds, 865-215-2330.

The city's property tax page lists these contacts side by side, and the county's Trustee page covers the county side.

What is Knoxville like, and how does it affect a sale?

Knoxville sits in the Tennessee Valley, roughly halfway between the Great Smoky Mountains and the Cumberland Plateau. James White founded the town in 1791, and it was incorporated in 1815. The city covers 104.2 square miles, about 98.5 of them land, and the Tennessee River runs through downtown as part of Fort Loudoun Lake after the Holston and French Broad rivers meet in the southeast.

Ridges give the city its shape. Elevations run from just over 800 feet along the riverfront to more than 1,000 feet on West Knoxville hilltops, with Sharp's Ridge in North Knoxville reaching 1,391 feet. The climate is humid subtropical, with just under 52 inches of precipitation a year and about 36 days at or above 90 degrees. Summers are hot and humid.

The housing stock follows the city's growth. Fourth and Gill, Parkridge and Fort Sanders grew up along the old streetcar lines and hold many Victorian and bungalow houses. Sequoyah Hills and Lindbergh Forest were early automobile suburbs with 1920s and 1930s styles. Bearden and Fountain City joined the city when it annexed them in 1962. Knox County Schools runs the public schools, with 89 schools according to Wikipedia, and the University of Tennessee's flagship campus is a steady source of renters and buyers. TVA, Pilot Flying J and the Discovery media networks have a base in the city, and I-40, I-75, I-640, I-275 and the Pellissippi Parkway (I-140) tie it together.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Knoxville city:

  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 202,021, up 6.0% from the 2020 base
  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 46.6%, so most households rent
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $239,700
  • Median gross rent: $1,191, with 86,263 households
  • Mean commute: 20.2 minutes

How is a Knoxville property tax bill figured?

The assessor appraises the property, applies a percentage set by use, and the taxing bodies multiply that assessed figure by their rates per $100. The assessor's guide lists the percentages: 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial, 30 percent for business personal property and 55 percent for public utilities. A house appraised at $100,000 therefore carries an assessed value of $25,000.

Knox County follows a two-year reappraisal cycle, so values are reset more often here than in counties on a longer cycle. In between, the assessor adds new construction and reviews part of the county each year. An Assessment Change Notice has to go out when a value or classification changes. The county commission and city council set the rates, not the assessor, and the city says it does not appraise anything itself.

Current city and county rates are not listed here, since they change with the budget. Ask the Revenue Office for the city rate and the Trustee for the county rate, or read both off the most recent bill for the parcel.

When is Knoxville property tax due, and is the discount still open?

City tax is due October 1 and turns delinquent on March 1 of the following year. Once March 1 passes, the city adds penalty and interest of 1 percent each per month.

The discount applies only to real estate tax, never to personal property or public utility tax. The city also applies each payment to the oldest unpaid year first, so a delinquent balance from a prior year absorbs money meant for the current bill. The Trustee takes county payments in person, online at propertytax.knoxcountytn.gov, by phone at 865-215-2305 option 3, or by mail. Its software vendor charges 2.5% on a credit card and $1.00 on an e-check, and the city's online payment fees likewise go to its vendor and not to the city.

How do I appeal a Knoxville assessment?

Begin with an informal talk with the assessor at 865-215-2360, then go to the county's equalization board if that fails. The assessor lists three valid grounds: your value is too high, another owner's value is too low, or the classification is wrong, such as commercial listed as residential. The amount of tax is never a ground, since the rate is not the assessor's decision.

The county board meets beginning June 1. A disputed assessment generally has to go there first or it becomes final. From the county board you can appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. The state board starts with a hearing before an administrative judge, who issues a decision within 90 days of the hearing. A taxpayer who still disagrees can petition a chancery court within 60 days after the state board's order becomes final. The Comptroller's appeals page walks through each step. This year's June window is closed, so an owner who missed it should wait for the next tax year's notice cycle.

What tax relief can a Knoxville homeowner claim?

The Trustee's relief page lists a state credit and a freeze. The credit pays part of the bill. It is not an exemption, so the full bill still arrives and the owner pays it.

  • Elderly and disabled homeowners: up to $85 for 2026, with combined 2025 income for all owners capped at $38,470.
  • Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers: up to $444, with no income limit, for an owner whose service-connected rating is permanent and total.
  • Senior freeze: owners 65 or older by December 31, 2026 can freeze the base tax on one home and up to five acres, with a 2025 income cap of $63,470 that counts VA income.

Each program needs a yearly application, and the Assessor's site gives April 5 as the apply-by date. The city's Revenue Office at 865-215-2084 also answers relief questions for city tax.

What happens to tax when a Knoxville house sells?

Tax stays with the house, whatever the contract says. The city states that unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even when the seller agreed to pay it, and that private agreements do not change the city's right to collect. A buyer should ask the Revenue Office for the bill on the parcel, and a seller who owes back tax should get the payoff figure early, from both the city and the Trustee.

Prorating is a matter between the buyer and seller, usually handled by the title company at closing. A seller with a balance, a pending appeal or an inherited house to clear can ask the title company how each item will appear on the settlement statement. Tennessee also holds tax sales for delinquent parcels: the Trustee's page shows a June 2, 2026 sale at the Grande Event Center on Clinton Highway, where bidders had to be current on their own taxes. Clearing an old balance before listing keeps a Knoxville house out of that process.

More questions about Knoxville, TN Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Knoxville collect the same tax as Knox County?

No, they are two separate taxes. The city bills its own rate through the Revenue Office and the county bills its rate through the Trustee. A house inside city limits normally receives both bills, and each office has its own phone number and payment address.

Can I still get the Knoxville city discount this year?

No. The full amount is due now, and delinquency begins March 1 of next year.

Who should I call if my Knoxville assessment looks too high?

Call the Knox County Property Assessor at 865-215-2360 for an informal review. That conversation is not an appeal, so to keep your rights, file with the county's equalization board, which sits beginning June 1.

Will a buyer owe my unpaid Knoxville tax?

Yes, the lien follows the property. The city says unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even if the seller promised to pay, so a title company usually collects any balance from your proceeds at closing.

How do I find out whether I qualify for relief on a Knoxville home?

Check the Trustee's relief page or call the Trustee at 865-215-2305. You must own the home and live in it, and income limits apply to the elderly and disabled credit and to the senior freeze. Applications are due by April 5.

Local notes

  • Tennessee structure: county Assessor of Property values; county Trustee collects county taxes; each city either collects its own levy or uses the county Trustee. Hamilton, Shelby, Knox, Davidson etc. differ as noted.
  • Tennessee: county Assessor of Property values property; county Trustee collects county taxes; cities either collect their own or contract with the county Trustee.
  • Nashville is a consolidated city-county (Metropolitan Government); the Metropolitan Trustee collects the combined real property tax.

Nashville by the numbers

With about 684,298 residents, Nashville is number 1 of the 28 Tennessee places in this guide by population (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). Census respondents put the median owner-occupied home in Nashville at $383,100, 37% above the Tennessee median for these places. Renters live in about 47% of Nashville homes, and owners in 53%, where the Tennessee median is 61% owners. A median build year of 1985 puts the typical Nashville house near 38 years old. These numbers describe Nashville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who sends the property tax bill in Nashville?

Two Metro offices share the job. The Assessor of Property decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Office of the Metropolitan Trustee mails the bill and takes the payment.

Nashville and Davidson County run as one Metropolitan Government, so the Trustee describes its role as the tax collector for the county. Besides real property, the office collects personalty and public utility taxes, runs the state tax relief, tax deferral and tax freeze programs, and handles delinquent taxes, Central Business Improvement District taxes, Gulch district taxes and vegetation liens. The Assessor's office is at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 210, Nashville, TN 37210.

  • Tax billing and collection, including payoff questions: 615-862-6330
  • Mortgage inquiries at the Trustee: 615-862-6330
  • Tax relief and tax freeze applications: 615-862-6140
  • Assessor call center for appeal appointments: 615-862-6059

How is a Nashville property tax bill figured?

The Trustee's calculator page lists four pieces: appraised value, assessment ratio, assessed value and tax rate. The assessor sets the appraised value. State law sets the ratio at 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial property and 30 percent for personalty.

The Metro Council sets the rate, and it is not final until the State Board of Equalization certifies it. The Trustee page shows two rates, each stated per hundred dollars of assessed value, one for the Urban Services District and one for the General Services District.

Source: Metropolitan Trustee, Calculate Property Taxes. The $417,400 line uses the Census median owner-occupied value for Davidson County as a stand-in, so your own bill will differ. Your appraisal notice and the Trustee's lookup show the real numbers.

When are Nashville property taxes due?

Statements go out in October, and the Trustee says the tax must be paid in full by the last day of February to avoid interest. For the bill mailed in October 2026, that means February 28, 2027.

You can pay at the Trustee's office or at a First Horizon Bank financial center, which accepts Metro property tax payments from October through February under an arrangement with the Trustee. If a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer normally pays the bill, but the Trustee's mortgage inquiry line can confirm whether a payment posted. Check this before you sign a sale contract, since a missed escrow payment becomes a closing item.

What is the path for contesting a Nashville property value?

You start with the Assessor and, if that fails, go to the independent Metropolitan Board of Equalization. For 2026 both windows have closed: the informal review deadline was April 17, 2026, and scheduling a formal appeal ended at 4:00 p.m. on June 26, 2026. Watch the Assessor's site next spring for the next dates.

The Board of Equalization is created under Metropolitan Charter Article 11, Chapter 2. It has five members appointed by the Mayor and confirmed by the Council, serving two-year terms, and it can send cases to hearing officers. It sits from the first business day of June until that year's equalization is finished. You book through the call center at 615-862-6059.

Bring evidence that supports a lower value as of January 1 of the appeal year:

  • Comparable sales close to your home in age, features and square footage, with size within about 20 percent of yours
  • Any fee appraisal you already hold, understood as an opinion that the board reviews rather than accepts automatically
  • Repair estimates for needed work, not routine upkeep
  • Photographs of damage or outdated kitchens and baths

A relative may file for the owner. Anyone else, including an attorney or tax representative, needs a signed letter of authorization that names the parcel and the assessment year. If the board's decision disappoints you, you have 45 days after the board mails its notice to go to the State Board of Equalization.

What tax relief can Nashville homeowners claim?

Homeowners aged 65 and up, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and surviving spouses of disabled veterans can apply for state-funded tax relief through the Trustee. The program dates to a 1973 constitutional amendment, and Metro adopted it locally.

The Trustee page for the current window lists an income cap of $38,470 for Davidson County, measured on 2025 income for all owners and a spouse. Applicants must have turned 65 by December 31 of the tax year, show the home is their principal residence, and sign a form that lets the Trustee check income with the IRS, Social Security or the state. Applications run through April 5, 2027, and anyone already enrolled in the relief or freeze programs must return a voucher by April 5 every year to stay in. Call 615-862-6140 before you gather paperwork, because the veteran and spouse routes use separate forms.

What happens when Nashville property tax goes unpaid?

After the last day of February, the bill becomes delinquent and interest applies under Tennessee law. The Trustee's office collects and processes delinquent taxes, so that office is where you ask for a payoff figure that includes interest through a specific closing date.

Liens also matter to a seller. The Trustee collects vegetation liens and the special district taxes mentioned above, so ask whether any of them sit on your parcel. A title company will search for all of them, and an early account history from the Trustee keeps a surprise charge from delaying closing.

How do you sell a Nashville house with tax still owed?

You can sell it. Unpaid property tax is cleared from the sale money at closing, and the title company asks the Trustee for the exact amount.

  • Call 615-862-6330 and ask for the balance, interest and any lien lines on your parcel.
  • Tell the closing agent the date you expect to close so interest is counted to that day.
  • If the house is vacant or inherited, confirm who the Trustee has on file to receive the bill, since a statement mailed to a former owner is easy to miss.
  • Compare any offer with the amount owed, because a low price can leave you short of the tax and loan balances.

Owners facing a large tax balance often weigh a sale to a buyer who closes as-is, which saves repair costs and showing time. Whatever route you choose, get the payoff in writing from the Trustee before you accept terms.

What do the Census numbers say about Davidson County homes?

Davidson County had 745,904 residents in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, a 4.2 percent rise over the 2020 base. It lists 389,379 housing units and 324,907 households for 2020 to 2024.

Only 52.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so close to half of the county's households rent. The median owner-occupied value is $417,400, owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,910, and median gross rent is $1,582. Median household income is $77,853. The county issued 5,632 building permits in 2025.

More questions about Nashville, TN Property Tax Guide

Is there a separate Nashville city tax on top of the county tax?

No. Nashville and Davidson County are one government, and the Trustee lists one rate for each service district: $2.814 in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District, each per hundred dollars of assessed value. Your tax bill shows which applies to your parcel.

By what date must 2026 Nashville property tax be paid to avoid interest?

The last day of February 2027, which is February 28. The Trustee mails statements in October and says taxes must be paid in full by that date to avoid interest.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Nashville property value?

No new appeal can start for 2026, because the informal review deadline was April 17, 2026 and the formal scheduling deadline was June 26, 2026. If you already had a Metropolitan Board of Equalization hearing, the state board accepts an appeal for 45 days after the notice is mailed.

Who qualifies for Nashville property tax relief?

Owners aged 65 and up, disabled owners, disabled veterans and surviving spouses of disabled veterans, if they meet the income limit. The Trustee lists $38,470 for Davidson County based on 2025 income, and applications are open through April 5, 2027.

Who do I call to find out what I owe before closing?

Call the Metropolitan Trustee's tax billing and collection line at 615-862-6330 and ask for a payoff that includes interest to your expected closing date. Hand the same figure to your title company so the balance comes out of what you receive at closing.

Who sends the property tax bills for a Chattanooga house?

Two governments bill every house inside Chattanooga city limits: Hamilton County and the City of Chattanooga. The appraisal comes from the Hamilton County Assessor of Property, the county bill is collected by the Hamilton County Trustee, and the city bill is the City Treasurer's job.

The city says plainly that an owner inside Chattanooga pays both. The Trustee also collects for Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Ridgeside, Soddy Daisy and Walden, but not for Chattanooga, so a bill from the Trustee will not cover the city share.

What dates control a Chattanooga tax bill?

Bills for the year go out in September, taxes are due from October 1, and payment without interest runs through the last day of February. Interest starts on March 1.

Hamilton County adds 1.5 percent for every month of delay, which it states as 18 percent annually. Chattanooga splits the same amount into 1 percent interest and a half percent penalty. Hamilton County adds that a mailed payment counts as late if the post office does not postmark it in time, while an online payment counts on the day of the transaction.

A stormwater fee rides on the city bill, so a payoff figure should include it. Partial payments post in a set order: stormwater fee interest first, then stormwater fee, then tax interest and penalty, then the tax itself.

Owners who are elderly, disabled or disabled veterans can apply for Tax Relief funded by the state, and the city runs a Tax Freeze that locks the bill at its first qualifying amount. A single Tax Relief application reaches both the city and county bills.

The city's 2026 notice sets a $38,470 ceiling on combined 2025 income for the elderly and disabled groups, with age 65 or disability required by December 31, 2026. You must pay the 2026 bill before the application can be processed, and the deadline to apply is April 5, 2027.

United Way will also cover the stormwater fee on the city bill for anyone approved for either program. Applicants who want help with the paperwork can call (423) 643-7274.

Begin with a call to the Assessor of Property at (423) 209-7300, and move on to the county Board of Equalization if that talk fails. The Tennessee Comptroller explains that skipping the county board generally closes off later appeals.

The county board usually opens its session on June 1. Beyond it sits the State Board, which takes appeals filed by August 1 or 45 days after the county board's notice goes out, whichever comes last. Ask the Assessor for this year's filing window.

Chattanooga lies on the Tennessee River at the Georgia border, where the ridge-and-valley Appalachians give way to the Cumberland Plateau. It spans roughly 150 square miles. The Census Bureau put the July 2025 population at 194,144, up from 181,099 in the 2020 count.

Ross's Landing became the city of Chattanooga in 1839, and the railroad arrived in 1850. The largest flood in its history came in 1867, before the Tennessee Valley Authority system existed. Today the economy runs on manufacturing and distribution, including the Volkswagen assembly plant that opened in 2011, plus insurance, health care and BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee on Cameron Hill.

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 count 79,084 households and a $283,200 median home value among owners, with median rent at $1,256. Just 52.4 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, so a seller may be dealing with tenants.

Ask the title company for a payoff of every open tax year before closing, and have county, city and stormwater amounts listed separately. Hamilton County states that unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property, so a balance does not vanish at transfer.

Past-due taxes, interest and any court costs are normally paid from the sale price at closing. If a bill is already with the Clerk and Master, request that office's figure, because it will differ from the Treasurer's. Recording the deed at the Hamilton County Register of Deeds follows the payoff, and the title company usually handles both steps.

Both bills go late on March 1, five months after the October 1 due date. After that, 1.5 percent is added to the unpaid amount each month.

Do I pay Chattanooga city tax and Hamilton County tax separately?

Yes, they are two bills with two collectors. The city share goes to the City Treasurer and the county share goes to the Hamilton County Trustee, and a payment to one leaves the other open.

Yes, if you are elderly, disabled or a disabled veteran. Chattanooga takes state Tax Relief applications and also runs a Tax Freeze. Applications for the 2026 year close April 5, 2027, after the bill itself is paid. Call (423) 643-7274 with questions.

The tax and any interest are still owed, since both governments say a missing bill excuses nothing. Look up the parcel on the city's search page or phone the Treasurer at (423) 643-7262.

Who do I call to dispute my Chattanooga assessment?

Phone the Assessor of Property at (423) 209-7300. An unresolved dispute goes to the county Board of Equalization, which normally sits from June 1.

Why does a Memphis house get two property tax bills?

Memphis sits in Shelby County, and each government taxes the same house on its own schedule. Yes, and the Shelby County equalization board opens its season on May 1, a month before the June 1 start common elsewhere in Tennessee. Tax year 2026 appeals ran May 1 through June 30, 2026, so that window is closed, and the next one opens in spring.

The board will not lower a value because a neighbor pays less, forgive late penalties, change rates or decide exemptions. Expect a written decision about two weeks after the hearing. What happens to unpaid taxes and city charges when a Memphis house sells?

The city lists weed cutting, demolition and board-up, sidewalk work and anti-neglect charges as items that can show up on the tax bill, so a house with a code history may carry more than the tax itself. Downtown properties may also face Central Business Improvement District taxes.

Delinquent real estate accounts go to attorneys on February 1 after a full year, and legal costs are added. Paying the balance from the sale proceeds at closing clears it first.

The Chancery Court orders the sale for cash, and the former owner, a lien holder or heirs have one year to redeem by paying taxes, interest, penalties and costs. The redemption price carries up to 10 percent interest a year. Except for state and federal liens, other liens are cleared by the sale. The city adds that the house can be sold at auction no matter who was supposed to pay under a contract, so a buyer's promise to pay does not protect the property.

What is Clarksville like for a homeowner?

Clarksville serves as seat of Montgomery County and is its sole incorporated municipality. It lies on the Cumberland River, anchors a metropolitan area that spills into Kentucky, and borders Fort Campbell. Its nickname is Queen of the Cumberland, and Austin Peay State University is in town. The Leaf-Chronicle, described as Tennessee's oldest newspaper, is published here.

Growth has been quick. The Census Bureau counted 132,929 people in 2010, 166,722 in 2020 and estimated 188,829 in July 2025, spread over about 99 square miles of land. Interstate 24 and U.S. Highway 79 carry much of the commercial growth, and the mean commute is 27 minutes.

The county Trustee points new owners to the closing statement to learn who pays for the year of transfer, and any unpaid tax stays on the property. A closing agent can request payoffs from the Trustee and the city and settle them out of the proceeds.

Ask for a calculation of the portion of the calendar year each party owns the house. The county Assessor posts a proration calculator that divides the year at a chosen date, which gives a starting number to compare with the closing statement.

Properties with taxes delinquent two or more years are eligible for the Montgomery County tax sale. After a sale the owner has a one year redemption period.

The Rutherford County Property Assessor appraises every parcel and prints the notices, and the City of Murfreesboro's Finance and Tax department collects the city share. The county's own share is collected by the Rutherford County Trustee, so a Murfreesboro owner has two payees.

  • Assessor's office: 319 N. Maple Street, Suite 200, Murfreesboro, TN 37130, phone (615) 898-7750. Use it for billing questions and to correct a mailing address.
  • City Finance Department: City Hall, 111 W. Vine St., first floor, phone (615) 893-5210, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • County Trustee: Historic Courthouse on the Public Square, phone (615) 898-7705.

Murfreesboro's property tax page explains that the city applies its rate to the county's assessed value, then the county mails the bills and the city collects its portion.

What kind of place is Murfreesboro for a seller?

Murfreesboro is the seat of Rutherford County and lies about 34 miles southeast of downtown Nashville, within the Nashville metro area of Middle Tennessee. The 2020 census counted 152,769 people, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 171,178, a 12.0% increase from the 2020 base.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $402,100, with $382,600 for Rutherford County.
  • Homes lived in by their owners: 52.4%.
  • Median household income: $80,108.
  • Median gross rent: $1,481.
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher: 43.0%.

The city covers about 63 square miles of land and has roughly 2,429 residents per square mile. The mean commute is 26.7 minutes. With a median home value above $400,000, a seller should know the exact tax owed before setting a price.

What does the 2026 reappraisal mean for a Murfreesboro tax bill?

Rutherford County runs a state-required countywide reappraisal every four years. The last one was in 2022, and the Assessor's FAQ says the next came in 2026. Values hold steady between those years except for new construction, additions, demolition or corrections.

A higher appraisal does not automatically raise the tax. Under Tennessee's certified tax rate law, a city or county must hold public hearings before adopting a rate that collects more in total than the year before. The Assessor adds that the tax rate is the County Commission's decision, not the Assessor's. The county's FAQ also explains that a lender's appraisal can differ from the Assessor's mass-appraisal value because a lender looks at one house in more depth.

The city's guidance on the calculation is simple: take the appraised value, multiply by 25 percent for residential property, 30 percent for business personal property or 40 percent for commercial, divide by 100, and multiply by the rate. The Trustee's FAQ lists the 2025 county rate as $1.8762 per $100. Because 2026 was a reappraisal year, ask the Trustee or the city for the rate printed on your current bill rather than reusing an old figure.

When is Murfreesboro city property tax due?

The city's October 2026 notice says tax is payable from October 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 without interest. Beginning March 1, 2027, unpaid base tax picks up 1.5 percent per month or any part of a month.

The city accepts cash, check or card, but not bank counter checks or two-party checks, and it takes partial payments. The county bill follows its own schedule: the Trustee's FAQ says it is due on the first Monday of October and can be paid until the last day of February without interest, and offers no early payment discount.

How do you appeal a Rutherford County valuation?

The first step is a phone call or visit to the Assessor at (615) 898-7750, where an appraiser reviews the property record with you. Errors in square footage or a listed defect are the usual topics at this informal stage.

If you still disagree, the next stop is a hearing before the Rutherford County Board of Equalization. Its appeals are normally held in June, with appointments starting the first week of May. The board's 2026 notice lists hearings starting July 7, 2026, at the Assessor's office, and that season has ended. The notice warns that skipping the county board makes the assessment final without further appeal.

After the county board, the State Board of Equalization is the next level. Its hearings begin before an administrative law judge, and an appellant must pay a state fee. The last step is a suit in Davidson County Chancery Court. Appeals do not delay the bill, so pay on time and request any refund afterward.

What property tax relief exists in Murfreesboro?

The state provides relief for elderly homeowners age 65 and over, for disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. The city page says the relief program is offered by both the City of Murfreesboro and Rutherford County, so an eligible owner files with both to cover the city and county bills. The deadline is 35 days after the city's delinquency date.

The Trustee's relief page adds a few specifics for veterans' households. A surviving spouse must have been married to the veteran at death and must not have remarried, and the property must be the applicant's primary residence. The page says the most market value used in the relief calculation is the first $175,000. Apply at the Trustee, (615) 898-7705, or the city tax office, (615) 893-5210.

Murfreesboro and Rutherford County have also approved the constitutional tax freeze for owners 65 and older. Contact the Trustee for forms. State relief does not erase the bill, and the Comptroller notes that it only reimburses taxes already paid.

How do you settle Murfreesboro property tax when you sell?

The Trustee's FAQ tells a new owner to read the closing statement or ask the title company who pays the year's tax, and states that unpaid tax continues to accrue against the property. Check both city and county balances rather than only one, since the Murfreesboro portion is billed separately from the county's.

Delinquent real property tax can be paid online through the Rutherford County Chancery Court's online services, which list delinquent amounts. A seller with an old balance should ask the Chancery Court clerk for a current payoff figure, because costs and interest change it.

When the house is vacant or inherited and the bill is overdue, the practical sequence is to confirm the amounts owed, tell the title company about each office, and have them paid from the proceeds at closing.

February 28, 2027 is the last day without interest. Bills were mailed and online payment opened October 1, 2026, and from March 1, 2027 interest runs at 1.5 percent per month.

Who do I call with a question about my Murfreesboro tax bill?

Call the Rutherford County Assessor at (615) 898-7750 for billing and address changes, and the City Tax Department at (615) 893-5210 for payments and relief programs.

Did Murfreesboro property values change in 2026?

Yes. 2026 was a countywide reappraisal year in Rutherford County, with the prior one in 2022. Under the certified rate rules, higher values do not necessarily mean a higher bill, so check the rate on your notice.

Can seniors get a break on Murfreesboro property tax?

Yes. The state's relief program covers qualifying owners 65 and older, disabled owners and disabled veterans, and Murfreesboro and Rutherford County also approved a tax freeze for owners 65 and over.

How do I pay Murfreesboro property tax online?

Use murfreesborotntax.com with a card or e-check. The processor adds about 2.5 percent plus $0.30 for cards or $1.50 for an e-check. The county portion is paid separately through the Trustee.

Jackson by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 68,098 people in Jackson, which makes it the 9th largest of the 28 Tennessee places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $195,000, 30% below the median of those 28 places. 52% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 48% are rented, against a median of 61% owner-occupancy across the Tennessee places. The median home was built in 1983, about 40 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Jackson as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Which offices handle property tax for a house in Jackson, TN?

Four offices touch a Jackson property tax bill. The Madison County Assessor of Property sets the value, the City of Jackson Revenue Office bills the city tax, and the Madison County Trustee bills the county tax. The county's own tax page says the Assessor takes no payments and mails no bills.

The Revenue Office sits in the west end of City Hall's first floor and keeps weekday hours from half past eight to half past four, closing on national holidays. City tax is paid at the customer service counter. For questions about city payments, call (731) 425-8212. The Trustee, Billy Burkhead, works from Suite 107 at 100 E. Main Street and can be reached at (731) 423-6027, with doors open nine to five. The Assessor, Frances Hunley, is upstairs in Suite 304 at (731) 423-6063, open from half past eight to five.

The Revenue Office also issues city business licenses, so a landlord with a rental in Jackson should ask there whether one applies. The City Recorder keeps ordinances, resolutions and deeds the city holds, and they can be viewed on request.

How does Jackson assess a home, and what rates apply?

The county's estimate calculator lists the assessment percentages below. A Jackson home is taxed on 25% of its appraised value, and the bill is the assessed value times the combined City of Jackson and Madison County rates.

Tax rates are set each year by the County Commission and the Jackson City Council, so use the calculator or the Revenue Office for the current figures. When is Madison County's next reappraisal and what has happened to values?

Madison County's next countywide reappraisal is scheduled for 2027, and the last one was in 2022, as required by Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-1601. Between reappraisals, about one third of parcels are inspected each year for changes to land or buildings.

The Assessor's page reports a median home sale price of $251,450 in January 2026, against $212,500 in January 2022, which it calls an estimated 18.33% increase. Assessment change notices go out by mail, usually in May, only to owners whose value moved up or down. Returned mail is common, so call the Assessor if you moved in the past two or three years.

  • Jackson owners should expect a notice in spring 2027 if their value changes.
  • The county advises owners to contact the Assessor first and confirm the property record is correct before appealing.

What is the appeal path for a Jackson assessment?

Start with a call to the Assessor to check the property record, then appear before the Madison County Board of Equalization. Its five members own property in Madison County or the City of Jackson, and they sit on weekdays through the first two weeks of June. You can book a slot in the last two weeks of May.

Only the current year's value is open to challenge: the county's example is that 2025 taxes cannot be appealed in 2026. A homeowner who loses at the county board can go to the State Board of Equalization. The county page gives the filing limit as August 1 or forty-five days after the date on the county's notice, whichever falls later. The state fee is partly nonrefundable, $10 to $17. Pay the undisputed part of the bill before it goes delinquent while the case is open.

Evidence the Assessor asks homeowners to bring:

  • Sales of similar nearby homes dated in the one or two years before the tax year under appeal.
  • A recent fee-based appraisal.
  • Photos of the exterior and interior condition.

What tax relief can Jackson homeowners apply for?

Elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans can apply through the Madison County Trustee. The Trustee's page asks applicants to bring a driver's license, Medicare card, Social Security card, proof of income for the applicant, spouse and all owners of the property, and a title or bill of sale if the home is a mobile home.

The county also lists a state property tax freeze program. The Tennessee Comptroller notes that relief reimburses taxes after you pay, so you still need to pay each bill, and that relief covers only your primary residence. Call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 for the current application period.

Online payment through the city covers real property, which is land and buildings, and personal property, which is business equipment. A homeowner will normally have only a real property bill and needs the parcel ID or street address to find it.

What does a seller owe at closing when a Jackson house has tax due?

The title company asks both the City Revenue Office and the Trustee for payoffs, since a home inside Jackson carries a city and a county bill. The Madison County page says homes within city limits should contact the City Revenue Office at (731) 425-8212 and also the County Trustee at (731) 423-6027, while homes outside the city deal with the Trustee alone.

The Assessor updates mailing addresses for both billing offices, so a new owner should ask the Assessor to change the address after the sale. For parcels outside Jackson, check whether the property sits in the City of Three Way or Humboldt, which the county calculator lists with their own rates.

If you do not know your parcel ID, the city's payment guide shows how to look up a property by address through the public records search.

What is Jackson like for a house seller?

Jackson is the Madison County seat, 70 miles east of Memphis and 130 miles southwest of Nashville. It was founded in 1821, named for Andrew Jackson, and became a railroad hub from 1851 onward. The Census Bureau estimates 69,339 residents for 2025, up from 68,205 in 2020, across about 58 square miles of land.

For 2020-2024 the Census Bureau shows 51.2% of Jackson homes occupied by owners, a $217,800 median value for those homes, $1,145 in median gross rent, and $53,032 in median household income. About 22.2% of residents live in poverty, and the city has 27,541 households. The average commute is 18.2 minutes.

Union University, Lane College and Jackson State Community College are in the city, and the Jackson-Madison County School System serves local students. Downtown has a designated Arts District with the Carl Perkins Civic Center nearby.

Where do I pay City of Jackson property tax?

Pay at the Revenue Office in City Hall on weekdays, or use the city's online portal for real and personal property. The phone number for city payment questions is (731) 425-8212.

Who collects Madison County property tax?

The Madison County Trustee, Billy Burkhead, collects it at 100 E. Main Street, Suite 107, Jackson. Call (731) 423-6027 to reach the office.

When is the next property reappraisal in Madison County?

The next countywide reappraisal is scheduled for 2027. The previous one took place in 2022. Notices of changed values are mailed by the Assessor, usually in May.

When can I appeal my Jackson assessment?

Use the Madison County Board of Equalization in the first two weeks of June, with appointments opening in late May. Only the current year's assessment can be appealed.

Does the Madison County Assessor send tax bills?

No. The Assessor sets values only and does not accept payments or mail bills. The City Revenue Office bills city tax and the County Trustee bills county tax.

Johnson City by the numbers

With about 71,455 residents, Johnson City is number 8 of the 28 Tennessee places in this guide by population (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). Census respondents put the median owner-occupied home in Johnson City at $238,000, 15% below the Tennessee median for these places. Renters live in about 50% of Johnson City homes, and owners in 50%, where the Tennessee median is 61% owners. A median build year of 1983 puts the typical Johnson City house near 40 years old. These numbers describe Johnson City as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who sends a property tax bill to a Johnson City homeowner?

Two bills can arrive. The city's Finance Department sends the city bill and takes the city payment, while the Washington County Trustee takes in the county tax on the same parcel. The city's property tax page gives the Municipal and Safety Building, 601 E. Main St., as the walk-in counter, staffed on weekdays from eight in the morning until five. Checks can go by post to Box 2227, Johnson City, TN 37605, and anyone with a late balance can reach the tax office at 423-434-6299.

The county side runs through two other offices. The Assessor of Property at 423-753-1671 handles appraisal and mailing address questions, while the Trustee at 423-753-1602 only collects. The Trustee's county tax page says plainly that it does not appraise property or set the rate.

Johnson City sits mostly in Washington County, with smaller pieces in Carter and Sullivan counties. A parcel in either of those slivers answers to that county's assessor and trustee, so read the county off your parcel record before dialing.

When is Johnson City property tax due this year?

The city says 2026 notices went out the week of October 12, and payment is due by February 28, 2027. The city will honor a postmark from that day or earlier, and penalty and interest begin accruing March 1, 2027. The county notice follows a similar track: the Trustee mails in October, takes payment through the end of February, and adds 1.5% interest to unpaid balances on March 1.

Tennessee owners are expected to pay whether or not a notice arrives. A homeowner whose lender pays from escrow will not receive a bill, so ask the servicer for proof of payment.

Ways to pay the city portion:

  • In person at 601 E. Main St. during weekday hours
  • By mail to the P.O. Box above
  • Online through the Finance Department's payment system, which adds a 2.75% processing fee per transaction

The city notes that online accounts past the due date are delinquent and cannot be paid online, and neither can taxes already filed in Chancery Court. For those balances call 423-434-6299 to confirm the exact payoff before sending money.

What kind of city is Johnson City, and how does that shape a sale?

Johnson City began in 1856 as a railroad stop called Johnson's Depot and was incorporated in 1869. Three rail lines crossed downtown at the peak, and the city later grew around East Tennessee State University, Ballad Health and the medical campus that includes Johnson City Medical Center and the VA hospital at Mountain Home. It sits in an Appalachian valley near Boone Lake on the Watauga River, and Buffalo Mountain, a ridge above 2,700 feet, is a city park on the south side.

Weather is a fact of life for older houses here. Rainfall averages about 45 inches a year and snow roughly 16 inches, which keeps roofs, gutters and crawl spaces working through damp summers and cold, wet winters. Most of the Washington County side is served by Johnson City Schools, whose campuses include Science Hill High School and University School, while a few edges fall under the county districts.

Census Bureau QuickFacts gives a picture of the housing stock:

  • A July 2025 estimate of 74,943 people, which is 5.5% above the 2020 base
  • 51.3% of homes lived in by their owners, leaving roughly half to renters
  • $268,200 as the typical value of an owner's home in the 2020 to 2024 survey
  • Rent near $1,023 a month and household income near $57,254
  • 20.3% of residents below the poverty line

With roughly half the households renting, a Johnson City seller may be a landlord with tenants in place, and the city and county balances for that rental should be pulled before an offer is signed.

How is the Johnson City tax amount figured?

Residential property is assessed at 25% of appraised value, and the rate is charged per $100 of that assessment. The Washington County Trustee's page walks through a $150,000 home: $37,500 of assessment multiplied by the county rate, with the final bill trimmed to whole dollars since tax year 2020. Its table lists a county rate of $2.15 per $100 under the heading 2023, so treat that number as dated and read the rate off your own 2026 notice.

The city adds its own rate on top for houses inside Johnson City limits. The city's page leaves the rate out, so City Finance is the place to get today's figure. Kingsport's own tax explainer mentions that Washington County values rose in 2024, so many owners here saw a new appraisal that year.

What can I do if I think my Johnson City assessment is wrong?

Start with the Washington County Assessor of Property at 423-753-1671. An informal review, where an assessor offers one, is only a conversation and does not count as an appeal, the Comptroller points out. The real first step is the board that hears county complaints, which sits in June, and a disputed value usually becomes final if that board is skipped.

Someone who loses at the county level can file with the state board by August 1, or 45 days after the county notice was sent if that falls later. On the state appeal page, the strongest proof for a house is a set of comparable sales with the differences explained. Saying the home is overvalued without numbers rarely works, and a jump after a countywide reappraisal is not itself proof of a mistake.

While the appeal is open, the undisputed share of the bill still has to be paid before it goes delinquent, along with any back taxes from earlier years.

Who pays the tax if a Johnson City house sells this winter?

Under the county's description, the tax roll shows whoever owned the property on January 1, so the seller often receives the bill even after a fall sale. The usual practice is to prorate at closing, after which the buyer carries the tax. The closing agent requests payoffs from the city and the Trustee and pays them out of the seller's proceeds.

When a bill is already late, get the payoff straight from the tax office, since online balances can trail payments still in transit. If the account has gone to Chancery Court, payment goes through the Clerk and Master and cannot be made on the city's website. A cash sale that closes quickly can clear those balances at the table, which helps when an inherited or tenant-occupied house has fallen behind.

When does the 2026 Johnson City tax bill go late?

Right after February 28, 2027. The city treats a postmark from that day as on time and starts penalty and interest March 1, 2027, and the county Trustee also takes county payments through the end of February.

Can I pay my Johnson City property tax online?

Yes, for current balances. The city charges a 2.75% processing fee per transaction. Delinquent accounts and taxes filed in Chancery Court cannot be paid online, so call 423-434-6299 for the exact payoff.

What if no county tax notice ever showed up?

Phone the Washington County Trustee at 423-753-1602. The county wants to hear from owners who have no notice by November 15, and the tax remains owed without one.

Does Johnson City tax apply to houses in Carter or Sullivan County?

The city bills its own tax inside city limits in every county, but the county portion goes to that county's trustee. Look up the county on your parcel record and contact that county's assessor and trustee for dates and rates.

Can a Johnson City house with back taxes be sold?

Yes, a sale can go ahead. Back city and county balances come out of the seller's proceeds, and the title company needs a current payoff from the tax office to do it.

Hendersonville by the numbers

With about 62,390 residents, Hendersonville is number 10 of the 28 Tennessee places in this guide by population (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). Census respondents put the median owner-occupied home in Hendersonville at $396,500, 42% above the Tennessee median for these places. Renters live in about 29% of Hendersonville homes, and owners in 71%, where the Tennessee median is 61% owners. A median build year of 1989 puts the typical Hendersonville house near 34 years old. These numbers describe Hendersonville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who sends a property tax bill to a Hendersonville homeowner?

A house inside Hendersonville is taxed twice, by Sumner County and by the City of Hendersonville, and the two bills come from different offices. The Sumner County Trustee collects the county share, and the city's finance office collects the city share. The Sumner County Assessor of Property sets the value both bills use.

Hendersonville is the largest city in Sumner County, on Old Hickory Lake about 18 miles northeast of Nashville. Its city hall is at 101 Maple Drive N, Hendersonville, TN 37075. The Trustee's office is in Gallatin at 355 North Belvedere Drive, Room 107, phone (615) 452-1260, open weekdays from eight to four-thirty. The Assessor can be reached at (615) 452-2412.

What are the Hendersonville and Sumner County tax rates?

The city's Tax Structure page lists a Hendersonville rate of $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value and a Sumner County rate of $1.4210 per $100. Together that is $2.0093 per $100 of assessed value. Residential and farm property is assessed at 25% of appraised value, commercial and industrial at 40%, and personal property equipment at 30%.

The Board of Mayor and Aldermen approves the city budget each year in a process of about three months, with two readings and a public hearing before it takes effect. That hearing is where a change in the city rate would surface.

Rates can change when the city and county adopt new budgets, so ask the finance office and the Trustee for the figures on your own bill. Census figures for 2020-2024 show a $430,700 median owner-occupied value in Hendersonville, so the example sits a little below a typical home here.

When is Hendersonville property tax due and how can I pay it?

City taxes can be paid from the first Monday in October and are due by the last day of February. Interest of 1.5% a month starts March 1. The county bill follows the same February deadline, and Sumner County adds interest from March 1 as well.

  • City bill by mail: send a check payable to the City of Hendersonville to 101 Maple Drive N. The postmark date counts as the payment date.
  • City bill in person: City Hall takes cash, check, money order or card, and a dropbox on the front portico is open around the clock for checks and money orders.
  • City bill online: through the city's online payment portal. Cards add a 2.95% convenience fee, and an e-check carries a $2.95 fee.
  • County bill: online at tnpayments.com, by mail with the top of the notice, by phone, at Room 107, or at local banks listed on the back of the notice. Cards cost 2.65% plus $1.

The Trustee takes up to five partial payments by check or cash. Any unpaid portion starts collecting interest on March 1.

How do I challenge a Hendersonville assessment?

Contact the Sumner County Assessor at (615) 452-2412 for an informal review, then use the Sumner County Board of Equalization, then the State Board of Equalization. For tax year 2026 the informal window ran May 4 to May 29 and the county board convened June 1. The last day to book a county board appointment was June 12, so that period is over.

The assessor's site says the next informal reviews should start in May 2027, with formal appeals for tax year 2027 heard from June 1, 2027. Sumner's last countywide reappraisal notices went out in 2024. The assessor lists the kinds of evidence it accepts for homes:

  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Recent photographs.
  • Insurance replacement value or a recent appraisal.
  • Costs to build, and the cost to cure any physical or functional problem.
  • Changes in the physical characteristics of the property.

Is there tax relief for Hendersonville homeowners?

Sumner County's Trustee runs the state relief program for elderly, disabled and disabled veteran homeowners, and also a tax freeze program for the county and part of the county's cities. Ask the Trustee whether the freeze covers your Hendersonville address, because the county describes it as covering only a portion of the cities.

Relief for people 65 and older and for disabled homeowners is income based. Relief for totally and permanently disabled veterans, and for their surviving spouses, is not. Applications are taken when the tax bills are mailed and must be finished no later than 35 days after the February payment deadline. Freeze applications for 2026 began in September 2026, and annual requalification is required. To book a phone or online appointment, call (615) 452-1260.

The Tennessee Comptroller adds that relief is a payment toward the tax, not an exemption, so you still receive and must pay your bills. Relief applies to a primary residence only.

What happens to property tax when a Hendersonville house sells?

Both the city and the county bill stay with the parcel, so the closing agent should pull a payoff from each office. Sumner County shows verification of paid taxes under the online payment link, which helps confirm that a prior year is clear.

The Assessor's office handles mailing address changes for county bills, so call (615) 452-2412 after closing so notices reach the new owner. Questions about tax sales in Sumner County go to the Clerk and Master's office.

Deeds are recorded with the Sumner County Register of Deeds, which publishes its own records site. Under state rules the grantee, meaning the buyer, pays the transfer tax.

What should a Hendersonville seller know about the city?

Hendersonville had 61,753 residents in the 2020 census and about 64,266 in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, the tenth largest city in Tennessee. The city has 25,255 households, and owners occupy 71.7% of homes. Rent runs a median $1,653, household income a median $97,200, and the mean commute is 29.7 minutes.

State Route 386 and U.S. 31E carry most traffic. A tornado struck the city on December 9, 2023, so ask for permit records on any house that had storm repairs. The city is governed by a mayor and twelve aldermen. Sumner County Schools serve Hendersonville, including Hendersonville High, Beech High, Ellis Middle and Merrol Hyde Magnet School.

Indian Lake Village, along Indian Lake Boulevard, is one of the city's main shopping and dining districts and mixes retail, offices, medical space and homes.

Hendersonville has roughly 47.9 inches of rain a year at the Old Hickory Dam station, with hot summers, so gutters and drainage are worth checking before you list.

More questions about Hendersonville, TN Property Tax Guide

Does Hendersonville have its own property tax?

Yes. The city levies $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value on top of the Sumner County rate of $1.4210. The city collects its own bill at 101 Maple Drive N, and the county Trustee collects the county bill in Gallatin.

When are Hendersonville property taxes due?

They are due by the last day of February. Payments open on the first Monday in October, and interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1. Mailed payments count on the postmark date.

How can I pay Hendersonville property tax online?

Use the online payment portal linked from the city's Tax Structure page. Cards carry a 2.95% convenience fee and e-checks a $2.95 processing fee, and both fees may change.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Hendersonville assessment?

No. The Sumner County Board of Equalization finished its 2026 session, and the last appointment day was June 12. Informal reviews for tax year 2027 are expected to start in May 2027.

Who do I call about senior tax relief in Hendersonville?

Call the Sumner County Trustee at (615) 452-1260. Applications are accepted when bills are mailed and until 35 days after the February deadline, and the office books appointments by phone or online.

Cleveland by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 48,185 people in Cleveland, which makes it the 16th largest of the 28 Tennessee places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $241,800, 13% below the median of those 28 places. 50% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 50% are rented, against a median of 61% owner-occupancy across the Tennessee places. The median home was built in 1982, about 41 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Cleveland as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who collects property tax on a house inside Cleveland city limits?

A house inside Cleveland gets two separate tax bills, one from the City of Cleveland and one from Bradley County. The Bradley County Assessor of Property values the parcel for both governments. Payment of the county bill goes to the Bradley County Trustee, and payment of the city bill goes to the city's finance office.

  • City of Cleveland Finance: Municipal Building, 190 Church Street NE, open weekdays until 5 in the afternoon. Phone (423) 472-4551, and mail to P.O. Box 1519.
  • Bradley County Trustee: 1701 Keith Street NW, phone (423) 728-7247. Monday through Thursday it keeps 8:30 to 4:30, and Friday it stays open until 5. Tim Akins was elected Trustee in 2026.
  • Bradley County Assessor of Property: (423) 728-7126, for address changes, values and appeals.

The county also takes calls on its toll-free automated payment line at (833) 591-7276.

When do Cleveland tax bills come due and when does interest start?

Cleveland mails its bills during the first week of October. Payment is due from October 1, and no penalty applies through February 28 of the following year. If payment is not received or postmarked by February 28, a 1.5 percent charge is added on the first of March and again each month after that.

The city's own page says that charge keeps building to a cap of 18 percent, which takes twelve months. After that, unpaid taxes pass to the Bradley County Clerk and Master. The Trustee's page asks owners to pay county tax by the end of February as well.

What is the Cleveland and Bradley County tax rate?

The county's net rate for 2025 is .9922 on each $100 of assessed value. The Trustee's FAQ shows two fire district surcharges that apply only to county-only properties: .2182 inside the fire fringe and .2408 outside it, which would not apply to a house inside Cleveland.

The Trustee does not publish the city rate on its FAQ and directs owners to the city office at (423) 472-4551, so ask for the current Cleveland rate when estimating a bill. Tennessee assesses residential property at 25 percent of appraised value. For a house at $272,200, the Census Bureau's median owner-occupied value in Cleveland, that means $68,050 of assessed value, and the .9922 county rate turns it into roughly $675 of county tax before any city charge.

What relief exists for Cleveland homeowners who struggle with the bill?

Bradley County runs the state Tax Relief program through the Trustee's office, and it also runs its own Tax Freeze for owners 65 and older. The City Clerk's office can take state relief applications at the Municipal Building as well.

  • Tax Relief reimburses part of the tax for elderly or disabled owners who live in the home. For 2025 the county brochure listed up to $81 for Cleveland city residents, $99 inside the fire fringe and $101 outside it.
  • Tax Freeze was adopted by the Bradley County Commission in August 2007. It holds the tax at the amount for the first year the owner qualifies, as long as the owner stays eligible and makes no improvements.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses can qualify for relief paid on the first $175,000 of home market value.

All taxes must be paid and current before relief is granted. The 2025 application deadline was April 5, 2026, so ask the Trustee for the 2026 deadline and income limit.

How do you challenge a Cleveland property valuation?

Ring the county Assessor of Property at (423) 728-7126 and request an informal look at the value. The Assessor's appraisal staff look at the file first, and a disagreement can go to the Board of Equalization, a panel of local citizens.

The city's finance page notes that appeals can be started at any time but are heard in the spring, and a decision affects only that year's tax. The Tennessee Comptroller states that county boards usually convene on June 1 and that an appeal to the county board keeps the right to go on to the State Board of Equalization.

What happens if Cleveland property tax is never paid?

The Bradley County Clerk and Master runs the annual tax sale on delinquent parcels, and the Trustee's office does not keep a mailing list. The county says sales are open public auctions, the notice list is published two to three weeks before the sale, and the price is paid in cash, money order or check at the time of sale.

A sale clears every lien except state and federal liens. The buyer waits a year from the filing of the sale confirmation before taking possession, and the former owner may redeem in that window. The buyer earns 10 percent a year during the redemption period. Contact the Clerk and Master at (423) 728-7209 for the next sale.

What should a Cleveland seller know about the local housing stock?

Cleveland holds the Bradley County seat and is the county's biggest city. Its incorporation dates to February 4, 1842. The 2020 census counted 47,356 residents, and the Census Bureau estimated 51,172 for July 2025, living on about 27 square miles of land.

The terrain is a series of parallel ridges, including Candies Creek Ridge, that extend the Appalachians north to south. Interstate 75 passes through the west side with three exits, the APD-40 beltway circles the business district, and Paul Huff Parkway is a major road on the north side. Lee University and Cleveland State Community College both operate here. Cleveland City Schools educates students who live inside the city limits, and Bradley County Schools maintains some campuses within the city as well.

Manufacturing anchors the local economy. Employers named for the area include Whirlpool, Mars, Procter and Gamble and Duracell. Figures for 2020 to 2024 show 18,829 households, $58,559 in median household income and a 21.3 minute average commute. Owners occupy 48.0 percent of homes and renters pay a median $1,034, so a seller may well have a tenant in place.

How should a Cleveland seller deal with tax owed at closing?

The county advises new owners to study the closing statement and ask the title company who pays, since responsibility turns on the transfer date and unpaid tax keeps accruing against the property. Ask the title company to pull both the county and city tax status before the contract date.

Cleveland's online system lets anyone verify that the current tax is paid, and the city office can supply a duplicate bill at (423) 472-4551. City partial payment agreements and payment plans only work if the balance is cleared before March, so a seller on one of those plans should ask the title company for a payoff figure instead of assuming the remaining installments transfer.

When is Cleveland property tax due?

The city bill is due starting October 1, and February 28 is the last penalty-free day. A 1.5 percent monthly charge begins in March and stops growing at 18 percent.

Who do I pay for property tax in Cleveland, TN?

Pay the City of Cleveland for the city tax and the Bradley County Trustee for the county tax. The city finance office is at 190 Church Street NE and the Trustee is at 1701 Keith Street NW.

Can I pay my Cleveland property tax in installments?

Yes, with limits. The city accepts partial payments if you complete forms and pay the whole amount before March 1, and it offers a twelve month plan if forms are in by February 15. Online card payments carry a 3 percent fee.

How do I appeal my Cleveland property value?

Start with the county Assessor at (423) 728-7126. If you still disagree after that review, the Board of Equalization takes the appeal in spring.

What if I leave a Cleveland property tax bill unpaid?

Interest climbs by 1.5 percent each month to a cap of 18 percent, and then the debt passes to the Bradley County Clerk and Master. Parcels still delinquent can go to a public auction, with one year to redeem.

Kingsport by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 55,807 people in Kingsport, which makes it the 12th largest of the 28 Tennessee places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $203,000, 27% below the median of those 28 places. 62% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 38% are rented, against a median of 61% owner-occupancy across the Tennessee places. The median home was built in 1974, about 49 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Kingsport as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

When is Kingsport property tax due, and is it past due now?

Anything unpaid becomes delinquent on December 1. The city's property tax page sets the penalties: 2% on December 1, another 2% on January 1, and 1% for each month after that until the bill is paid.

City statements are mailed between mid September and mid October, once the state approves the assessments, and values are set as of January 1. Payments can be mailed, put in the night deposit box, or made at the Customer Service Center in City Hall at 415 Broad Street. Questions go to 423-343-9860.

The county bill is a separate calendar. The Sullivan County Trustee says county tax is due the first Monday in October and can be paid without penalty through the last day of February. A Kingsport homeowner can therefore be holding a November 30 city deadline and a February county deadline at the same time.

Who handles Kingsport property tax besides City Hall?

The Sullivan County Property Assessor sets the value, and the Sullivan County Trustee collects the county portion. The Trustee's FAQ lists a main office at 1651 Blountville Boulevard in Blountville, 423-323-6464, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A Kingsport satellite office at 225 West Center Street, Suite 101, takes payments Monday through Wednesday from October 1 to March 15 at 423-354-7036, and it closes from mid March through September.

Kingsport also reaches into Hawkins County, so a house in that part of the city belongs to the Hawkins County assessor and trustee. Ask the Hawkins County Trustee for that county's own dates and rate.

Sullivan County also posts these points for taxpayers:

  • The county mails a courtesy notice, but Tennessee does not require one
  • Installments are allowed between October 1 and February 28, and the owner tracks the balance
  • Cards carry a 2.5% fee and e-checks a $1.25 fee
  • Interest runs at 1.5% per month from March 1, and payment is accepted through March 15 before the account moves to the Clerk and Master

What are the Kingsport and Sullivan County tax rates?

The City of Kingsport lists a 2025 rate of $1.67 per $100 of assessed value, down from $1.99 for 2024. Sullivan County's FAQ gives a 2025 county rate of $1.6129. The city explains the change: the state's two-year ratio appraisal cost Kingsport about $3.8 million a year in revenue, Sullivan County reassessed in 2025 for the first time since 2021, and the city's fiscal 2026 budget took effect July 1.

Here is how the arithmetic works for a house appraised at $200,000. Residential property is assessed at 25%, so the assessment is $50,000. At the city rate that gives $835, and at the county rate it gives about $806. These are illustrations only; the rates on your own notice control.

What is Kingsport like for a homeowner?

Kingsport lies along the Holston River in western Sullivan County and extends into Hawkins County and north to the Virginia line. It sits where U.S. 11W and U.S. 23 meet, and it is the northwest end of Interstate 26. The city covers about 51 square miles and was chartered in 1822, then re-chartered in 1917 when it adopted the council-manager system it still uses.

Eastman Chemical Company has its headquarters and first plant in the city, much of it on Long Island in the Holston. Domtar runs a recycled containerboard mill, and the Holston Army Ammunition Plant manufactures explosives for the Department of Defense. Kingsport City Schools serve almost every resident, with Dobyns-Bennett High School as the main high school. Neighborhoods include Lynn Garden, Bloomingdale, Colonial Heights, Rock Springs, Highland Park and Orebank, among others.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Kingsport:

  • 57,530 residents on July 1, 2025, up 3.6% from April 2020
  • Owner-occupied rate of 60.1% and 25,021 households
  • Median owner-occupied home value of $234,100 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent of $907 and median household income of $52,490
  • 23.3% of residents are 65 or older, the highest share among the places compared

The city and the state both run relief programs aimed at senior and disabled owners, covered below.

How does a Kingsport owner dispute a higher value?

Values follow a yearly cycle that the Tennessee assessment calendar spells out. Ownership and condition are fixed as of January 1, change notices are due out by May 20, and the county board of equalization meets from June 1 through the month. Because Sullivan County reassessed in 2025, many Kingsport owners saw a new number that year, and the 2026 appeal window has already closed for most of them.

The next steps for someone who disagrees with a value:

  • Call the Sullivan County Assessor before the next June board meeting and ask whether an informal review is offered
  • File with the county board of equalization, since skipping it generally ends later appeal rights
  • Gather sales of similar Kingsport houses, with differences in age, condition and size explained
  • Pay the undisputed part of the bill on time while the dispute is open

Are there relief programs for Kingsport homeowners?

The city notes that a relief program exists for elderly or disabled homeowners within income limits, and links a brochure and the state Comptroller's relief page. Sullivan County states it does not offer a Tax Freeze program, so relief is the route there. A relief voucher for an owner with a mortgage must be signed and returned by April 5 each year or the state voids the credit.

For the dispute process, the state's appeal rules start at the county board of equalization, and the Sullivan Assessor can say when it sits.

What if I sell a Kingsport house with the tax unpaid?

Sullivan County's guidance is that the owner of record on January 1 gets the notice, and a buyer who closes later is still responsible for making sure tax is paid on time. The settlement statement is where the split is written down. If the November 30 city deadline passes before closing, the city penalty and the county interest grow every month, so a payoff request should be dated close to the closing day.

Unpaid tax is settled from the seller's proceeds at the table. Call the city at 423-343-9860 and the Trustee in Blountville for written payoffs.

What happens if I miss the November 30 Kingsport deadline?

A 2% penalty applies on December 1, another 2% on January 1, and 1% each month after until you pay. Mail, the night deposit box and the City Hall counter at 415 Broad Street are all accepted.

Is the Kingsport city rate going up or down?

The 2025 city rate is $1.67 per $100, lower than the $1.99 listed for 2024. The city ties the shift to the state's ratio appraisal and the 2025 Sullivan County reassessment.

Where do I pay the Sullivan County part of my Kingsport tax?

Pay the Sullivan County Trustee in Blountville or at the Kingsport satellite office on West Center Street, which is open Monday through Wednesday from October 1 to March 15. Online and phone payments add card or e-check fees.

Does Kingsport have a tax freeze for seniors?

Sullivan County says it does not offer a Tax Freeze program. The state tax relief program is available for eligible elderly and disabled owners, and the voucher goes back by April 5.

Can a Kingsport house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes. Unpaid city and county balances are paid from the seller's proceeds at closing. Get written payoff figures from the city and the county Trustee before the closing date.

Collierville by the numbers

Collierville has roughly 51,212 residents in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, and ranks number 15 by population among the 28 Tennessee places in this guide. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $458,300 here, which is 64% above the middle figure for the 28 Tennessee places. About 19% of households rent, so 81% own; the Tennessee median for these places is 61% owner-occupied. Homes here were typically built in 1997, so the median house is about 26 years old. These numbers describe Collierville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who sends the property tax bill in Collierville?

Collierville owners deal with two taxing bodies, the Town of Collierville and Shelby County. The town's tax department takes questions at 901-457-2281 or propertytax@colliervilletn.gov, and its Taxes page notes that residents also owe county tax.

Within the county system, the Assessor of Property establishes value, the Board of Commissioners picks the county rate, and the Trustee prints notices and mails them to whatever address the Assessor holds. Where a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer may ask for the figures and pay, and the Trustee advises borrowers to hold on to the original notice anyway.

Since the notice follows the Assessor's mailing address, someone who has moved should update it well before October.

What is the Collierville tax rate and how is a bill figured?

The town's Taxes page gives its rate as $1.62 for each $100 of assessed value. Tennessee assesses homes at 25% of appraisal, so a $100,000 house is $25,000 on the roll and owes $405.00 to the town.

The same page also lists 40% for commercial and industrial parcels, 55% for public utilities, 25% for farms and 30% for personal property. The Trustee or the Assessor can tell you the Shelby County rate to add on top. Using the Census Bureau's $485,900 median owner-occupied value as a sample house, assessed value is $121,475 and the town share lands near $1,968.

When are Collierville property taxes due and when do they go delinquent?

Shelby County taxes open on the first Monday of October and stay interest-free until the end of February.

The Trustee's interest page puts Collierville in the group whose bills turn delinquent March 1. Unpaid base tax then gains 1.5% a month, which the Trustee states as 18% a year. A mailed check counts when postmarked by the final day of February, and the stub of your notice goes with it to the Shelby County Trustee, P.O. Box 2751, Memphis, TN 38101-2751.

Call Trustee customer service at (901) 222-0200 with account questions. Under Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-2405 the Trustee must sue to collect delinquent real estate tax, and a tax lien stays until the full balance is paid.

How do you challenge a Collierville assessment?

The first stop is an informal review with the Shelby County Assessor, followed by a Board of Equalization filing if you still disagree. The Assessor stresses that an informal review is not an appeal. It lets you hand over information so the value tracks the market.
